p.PROTOCOL-STATEMENT: A capability lives in a library. Every way a user or an agent reaches it — command line, TUI, MCP server, HTTP API — is a **surface**: thin, replaceable, and never the place the capability is defined.

why.title: Why this is a discipline and not a preference

p.THE-SECOND-SURFACE-IS-WHERE-IT-HURTS: The cost never appears when the first surface is written. It appears when the second one is, because the logic is already inside the first — so the second either reimplements it or reaches into a place that was never meant to be an interface.

p.TWO-SURFACES-THAT-DIVERGE-ARE-INDISTINGU: Two surfaces of one capability that answer differently are indistinguishable from a bug, and nobody can say which one is wrong without a third place to appeal to. That third place is the library.

p.THE-DIVERGENCE-IS-SMALL-AND-SILENT: The divergence is usually small enough to survive review — a path separator, a rounding, a default — which is exactly why it needs a structural answer rather than care.

placement.title: Where this belongs, and where it does not

p.THIS-IS-ABOUT-DELIVERY-NOT-ABOUT-CODE-ST: This flow is about **how a capability reaches its user**. It is not a code-style rule and it is not part of any language discipline: a project writing no AI-native code at all still has surfaces and still pays for letting them diverge.

p.IT-IS-INSTALLED-BY-CHOICE: It is installed by a project that wants it, like every other cross-cutting practice in this group — git practices, addressable specs, campaign plans, source mirrors.

p.ONE-LIST-SO-EVERY-PROJECT-MEANS-THE-SAME: One list, so that two projects mean the same thing by the same word:

td.fact: not a surface; what the others sit on. Mandatory once there is more than one surface
rendering one dataset into different views for a human present at the machine
tool description, schema, and what an agent can discover without being told
contract versioning and compatibility with clients you do not deploy

p.THE-CLASS-IS-THE-USEFUL-UNIT: The class, not the individual surface, is the useful unit: it decides what repeats and therefore what belongs in the library versus what each surface legitimately does for itself.

p.THIN-IS-DEFINED-PER-CLASS-NOT-GLOBALLY: "Thin" cannot be one rule, because the classes fail differently:

item.THIN-LOCAL: **local** — the surface may own presentation entirely: column widths, colour, paging, progress. It may not own a decision. If removing the surface would lose a rule about *what is true*, the rule is in the wrong place.

item.THIN-AGENT: **agent-facing** — the surface owns its description and schema, and those are part of the surface, not of the library: an MCP tool's prose is written for a reader the library never sees. It owns nothing else.

item.THIN-NETWORKED: **networked** — the surface owns its wire contract and its version policy. It may translate; it may not compute.

p.THE-TEST-IS-DELETION-OF-THE-SURFACE: The test that settles arguments: **delete the surface on paper.** If anything but presentation and transport is lost, the split is wrong.

p.A-PROJECT-DECLARES-WHICH-SURFACES-IT-OWE: A project declares which surfaces it owes. The declaration is the whole point: without it, "should this have an MCP tool?" is answered per capability, by whoever is writing it, differently each time.

p.AN-UNDECLARED-SURFACE-IS-NOT-A-DEBT: **An undeclared surface is not a debt.** A project with no LSP has not failed to build one; it has not chosen to. This is what keeps the vocabulary from reading as a checklist of things everyone owes.

p.A-NEW-CAPABILITY-IS-BORN-WITH-THE-DECLAR: A new capability ships with every declared surface, or with a recorded reason why one sufficed — recorded where the capability is specified, not in a plan.

p.A-HAND-KEPT-COVERAGE-TABLE-ROTS: A table listing which capability has which surface must not be hand-maintained. It is a restated fact, and a restated fact diverges from what it restates — reliably, and without announcing it.

p.THE-VOCABULARY-IS-MACHINE-READABLE-SO-TH: Therefore the vocabulary is machine-readable, and the table is a **query** over what the project already knows: its command surface, its registered agent tools, its routes. Deriving it is a separate build; being able to derive it is a property of this vocabulary.

item.NEVER-DEFINE-A-CAPABILITY-INSIDE-A-SURFA: Never define a capability inside a surface.

item.NEVER-TREAT-ONE-SURFACE-AS-THE-REFERENCE: Never treat one surface as the reference the others are ported from — the library is the reference, or there is none.

item.NEVER-LET-TWO-SURFACES-ANSWER-DIFFERENTL: Never let two surfaces answer one question differently; when they do, the fix belongs in the library, not in whichever surface was reported.

item.NEVER-READ-THE-VOCABULARY-AS-A-CHECKLIST: Never read the vocabulary as a list of surfaces every project owes. It is a naming scheme; the floor is the project's own declaration.
